## objective
own auth build (spec review waived by the human): Supabase Auth, own Account screen, withSession, Settings account section

Auth is Supabase Auth on the existing project (ref hrwhjngmrdoxkxgnlrra), with sign-in screens we draw ourselves in the app's design. Work in your own worktree from goal/T-0001 (head fb2f47c). Run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` first; add the one new dependency with `pnpm add @supabase/supabase-js` (pnpm-lock.yaml stays the only lockfile). No Clerk package, no other new dependency.

Read first: src/App.tsx, src/main.tsx, src/screens/Settings.tsx (keep the T-0034 glass styling and the T-0037 Gemma licence line untouched), src/screens/Settings.test.tsx, src/test/setup.ts, src/sync/schema.ts, src/styles or tokens file used by T-0034, docs/SUPABASE.md, .env.example, README.md.

1. src/sync/supabase.ts
   - `getSupabase()` returns ONE memoised supabase-js client from VITE_SUPABASE_URL + VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY with auth options {persistSession: true, autoRefreshToken: true, detectSessionInUrl: false, storageKey: "alltag.auth"} (localStorage works in the Capacitor webview); null when either var is missing.
   - `isSupabaseConfigured()`.
   - `withSession<T>(fn: (client, userId: string) => Promise<T>): Promise<T | null>`: returns null WITHOUT calling fn unless configured AND `client.auth.getSession()` yields a session; otherwise calls fn with the client and session.user.id. This is the only door for the sync task: signed out means no network at all.
   - `__resetSupabaseForTests()`.
2. src/auth/auth.tsx
   - Context default DISABLED = {status: "disabled", userId: null, address: null, signIn, signUp, signOut, resetError, error: null} where the functions resolve to {ok: false, error: "off"}.
   - `AuthProvider`: not configured -> provides DISABLED, no network. Configured -> status "loading" until the first `getSession()` resolves, then "signed_in" (userId = user.id, address = user.email) or "signed_out"; subscribes to `onAuthStateChange` and unsubscribes on unmount.
   - `signIn(address, password)` -> supabase.auth.signInWithPassword; `signUp(address, password)` -> supabase.auth.signUp; returns {ok, needsConfirm, error}. needsConfirm = true when signUp returns a user but no session (project requires confirming the address). `signOut()` -> supabase.auth.signOut(). Map errors to calm copy: invalid credentials -> "that address and password don't match"; user exists -> "there is already an account for this address, sign in instead"; weak password -> "use at least 8 characters"; network/fetch -> "no connection, try again when you are online"; anything else -> "something went wrong, try again".
   - `useAuth()` reads only the context.
   - main.tsx wraps <App/> in <AuthProvider>.
3. src/screens/Account.tsx (our own sign-in UI, no third-party widgets): a sheet/screen in the T-0034 design language (paper ground, large title, glass close button, moss primary capsule, calm lowercase copy). Two modes switched by a segmented control: "sign in" and "create account". Fields: address (<label>, type email, autocomplete email/username) and password (<label>, type password, autocomplete current-password or new-password), a show/hide password toggle button with aria-label. Client validation before calling: address must contain "@" and a dot after it, password at least 8 characters; inline error line under the fields (role="alert"). Primary button text "sign in" / "create account", disabled while pending with a spinner. Below: "not now" text button that closes. Footnote: "optional. without an account everything stays on this phone. your words sync to an EU server (Supabase)." After needsConfirm: replace the form with "check your inbox to confirm your address, then sign in here." and a "back to sign in" button. On success: close and return to Settings.
   - Reachable from Settings (and from onboarding's "I have an account" link if onboarding has one; if not, skip). Use whatever routing/overlay pattern App.tsx already uses for screens.
4. Settings: an "account" section above the offline tutor section. disabled -> muted "sync is off in this build". loading -> muted "checking your account…". signed_out -> "sign in to sync your words, scenes and conversations across devices. everything also works without an account." + primary moss capsule "sign in" opening Account. signed_in -> the address, "signed in", a "sync" row reading "ready" (U3 fills it), secondary "sign out".
5. Docs and config: docs/SUPABASE.md replaces every Clerk mention with a Supabase Auth section (email + password, the "Confirm email" project setting and what the app does in each case, no redirect URLs needed because there are no magic links, sessions stored on the device under alltag.auth, sign-out keeps local data). .env.example: delete the Clerk line; the anon key comment says "RLS on auth.jwt() sub protects the data". README env list: drop Clerk. supabase/config.toml: if it has an [auth] section, set `site_url` unchanged and add `[auth.email] enable_signup = true` only if absent (do not change other keys).
6. Tests (mock @supabase/supabase-js createClient locally per file with vi.hoisted spies; no global mocks in src/test/setup.ts):
   - src/sync/supabase.test.ts: null when unconfigured; one client; withSession does not call fn without a session; calls fn with userId when a session exists.
   - src/auth/auth.test.tsx: no env -> disabled and createClient never called; configured -> loading, then signed_in after getSession; onAuthStateChange sign-out flips to signed_out; unsubscribe on unmount; signIn/signUp map the five error cases; needsConfirm when signUp returns no session.
   - src/screens/Account.test.tsx: validation blocks bad address and short password without calling signIn; signIn called with the typed values; error line renders the mapped copy; create-account with needsConfirm shows the confirm message; "not now" closes.
   - Settings.test.tsx: the four account states by wrapping in the auth context with test values; existing Settings tests stay green unchanged (they render outside AuthProvider and get DISABLED).
Finish: `npm test -- --watch=false`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npm run lint`, `pnpm build`. `git grep -n -i clerk -- src docs .env.example README.md` must find nothing. Commit as "U2 v4: own auth with Supabase Auth (password), our own sign-in screen, withSession for sync" and report `git diff --name-only HEAD~1`.

AMENDMENTS from spec review T-0057 (binding; where they conflict with the text above, these win):
B1 Live project facts (Planner, 2026-10-10): the human turned OFF address confirmation on the Supabase project, so signUp returns a session and signs the user in at once. The project region is eu-central-2, which is ZURICH: footnote copy says "your words sync to a server in Zurich (Supabase)", never "EU". Clerk third-party auth was never enabled on the live project, so there is no live-side change in this task.
B2 supabase/config.toml: delete the whole [auth.third_party.clerk] block (and any CLERK_DOMAIN env reference); then add `[auth.email] enable_signup = true` only if absent; set `enable_confirmations = false` under [auth.email] to match the live project. Change no other key.
B3 Clerk wording: fix comments only, no SQL or behaviour change: src/sync/schema.ts (line 7 says the Clerk sub -> "the auth user id (JWT sub)"), the comment lines in supabase/migrations/20261010120000_init.sql, and the test title in supabase/migrations.test.ts. All three are added to scope. The acceptance grep becomes `git grep -n -i clerk -- src docs supabase .env.example README.md` finds nothing. The T-0038 depends_on text mentioning Clerk is history, not a requirement.
B4 Account placement: local overlay state in App.tsx (`accountOpen` boolean), opened from Settings through a prop or a tiny event in src/auth/auth.tsx (`openAccount()` via context). Do NOT touch src/lib/screen.ts or TabBar. The tab bar is hidden while Account is open (Account renders full-screen above it). src/screens/Onboarding.tsx is removed from scope; do not create it.
B5 signUp result: if `data.user` exists and `data.user.identities?.length === 0`, return {ok: false, needsConfirm: true} with the same neutral copy as the confirm case ("check your inbox to confirm your address, then sign in here."), never "already exists" (no account enumeration). B7 withSession: wrap getSession in try/catch and return null on failure; errors thrown by fn propagate unchanged. Doc comment: reads the stored session, does not verify it online.
B8 Tests mechanics: vi.stubEnv + vi.unstubAllEnvs in afterEach, `__resetSupabaseForTests()` in beforeEach, vi.hoisted spies per file, no global mocks in src/test/setup.ts. Add a React.StrictMode double-mount test proving exactly one live onAuthStateChange subscription after mount/unmount/mount.
B9 Account.tsx: block double submit while pending; clear the password field on success and on mode switch; "back to sign in" after needsConfirm; mode switch keeps the typed address.
B10 Rollback note in the result: revert the commit and `pnpm remove @supabase/supabase-js`; no live-side state to restore.
Acceptance adds: identities-empty test; code-based mapping tests; StrictMode subscription test; widened clerk grep is empty.

C1 Applied migration stays untouched: do NOT edit supabase/migrations/20261010120000_init.sql or supabase/migrations.test.ts (their Clerk comments are history). Do fix the comment on line 1 of supabase/seed.sql and the src/sync/schema.ts comment. The clerk grep is `git grep -n -i clerk -- src docs .env.example README.md supabase/config.toml supabase/seed.sql` and must find nothing.
C2 Existing address on sign-up: address confirmation is OFF on the live project, so Supabase answers a duplicate sign-up with error code user_already_exists (or email_exists). Map both to "there is already an account for this address. sign in instead." and switch Account to sign-in mode keeping the typed address. Only when signUp returns a user with `identities?.length === 0` (happens only if confirmation is turned back on) use the neutral "check your inbox to confirm your address, then sign in here." with "back to sign in".
C3 Account lives inside AuthProvider: AuthProvider owns `accountOpen` state and renders <Account onClose=...> as a full-screen overlay above its children when open. The context gains `openAccount()` and `closeAccount()`; DISABLED has no-op versions. Settings calls `useAuth().openAccount()` (no props). App.tsx needs no change beyond what main.tsx wrapping requires; remove App.tsx edits if none are needed. Escape key on the Account root (onKeyDown on the overlay element, not a global listener) and "not now" both close. Account unmounts on sign-in success. Results that resolve after close are ignored (mounted ref).
C4 Status source: status comes ONLY from onAuthStateChange. supabase-js v2 emits INITIAL_SESSION on subscribe; until the first event, status is "loading". Do not call getSession for status. The callback is synchronous: no await and no other supabase call inside it (supabase-js deadlocks otherwise); it sets state from the event's session only.
C5 getSupabase() and isSupabaseConfigured() read import.meta.env at CALL time, never at module load, so vi.stubEnv + __resetSupabaseForTests work. withSession still uses getSession (stored session, not verified online) inside try/catch.
C6 No stray lockfile: after `pnpm add @supabase/supabase-js`, `git status --short` shows no package-lock.json.
THE ACCEPTANCE LIST OF THIS TASK REPLACES all earlier acceptance text.

AMENDMENTS from spec review T-0061 (binding; they win over everything above):
D1 README: update the sentence that counts the VITE_ vars (it says "these three VITE_ vars") to the new count and list; docs/readme.test.ts requires every .env.example var to appear in README.md, keep that true. docs/readme.test.ts itself is not edited.
D2 supabase/config.toml: also remove the CLERK_DOMAIN header comment; the file has no [auth.email] section today, so add `[auth.email]` with `enable_signup = true` and `enable_confirmations = false`.
D3 Loading fallback: if no auth event arrives within 4000 ms of subscribing, call `getSession()` once OUTSIDE the event callback and set signed_in/signed_out from it; if that throws, set signed_out. A later auth event always wins over the fallback. Test with fake timers.
D4 Results vs events: signIn/signUp return values drive the Account UI (ok -> close the overlay); the provider status flips only from the auth event. Settings shows the new status as soon as the event lands. Tests assert both: the returned ok closes Account, and an emitted SIGNED_IN event sets signed_in.
D5 Mapping order: first the code checks (invalid_credentials; user_already_exists or email_exists; weak_password), then retryable fetch error or status 0 (offline copy), then the generic copy.
D6 withSession: if the stored session expires within 30 s (session.expires_at * 1000 < Date.now() + 30000), call `client.auth.refreshSession()` first and use its session; if refresh fails or yields no session, return null without calling fn. Test the expired path.
Acceptance adds: loading fallback test with fake timers; expired-session refresh test; mapping order test (a weak_password error with status 0 still maps to the weak password copy).

SPEC REVIEW WAIVED by the human (2026-10-10 15:55). Build exactly the spec above, including every amendment; where spec review notes on T-0063 point at real defects you can fix inside scope, fix them and list them in your result. Known ones: (1) per-file vi.mock of @supabase/supabase-js must spread `await vi.importActual(...)` so isAuthRetryableFetchError stays real; (2) export AuthContext from src/auth/auth.tsx so Settings.test.tsx can wrap Settings with test values; (3) in withSession treat a missing or non-numeric expires_at as expiring and refresh; (4) the D3 fallback getSession is bounded by its own 3 s timeout and falls back to signed_out offline; (5) README counts the VITE_ vars correctly (VITE_API_BASE included). Out of scope here: what happens to local rows when a different user signs in (the sync task owns that).

    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args.     description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Supabase and Supabase Auth

The app works fully signed out and offline. Local storage is the source of truth on the device. An account only adds sync: signed in, the app pushes and pulls rows and scene photos to Supabase.

## How the pieces fit

- **Supabase Auth is the identity provider.** The app signs in with email and password through supabase-js, on screens we draw ourselves (`src/screens/Account.tsx`). No third-party widget.
- **RLS keys everything on the JWT sub.** `public.current_user_id()` returns `auth.jwt()->>'sub'`, which Supabase Auth fills with the user id (a uuid). Every table has `user_id text` defaulting to it, and one policy per operation allows only `user_id = public.current_user_id()`. The anon role has no access.
- **Storage.** Private bucket `scenes`. Path convention: `<sub>/<sceneId>.jpg`. Storage policies allow a user only objects whose first folder is their sub. `scenes.image_path` stores that path.
- **Sync columns.** Every table has `updated_at` (set by the `set_updated_at` trigger) and `deleted_at` (soft delete), indexed on `(user_id, updated_at)` so a pull is "my rows changed since t".

| table | key | what |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `profiles` | `user_id` | level (A1 to B2), display name, settings |
| `items` | `id` uuid | kept phrases and SM-2 state in `srs` (interval, ease, reps, due) |
| `scenes` | `id` uuid | captured place, objects, task, photo path |
| `conversations` | `id` uuid | roleplay transcript lines, duration, kept count |

Row types for the client: `src/sync/schema.ts` (`ProfileRow`, `ItemRow`, `SceneRow`, `ConversationRow`, `TABLES`, `BUCKET`). The SQL is `supabase/migrations/20261010120000_init.sql`.

## Supabase Auth

- **Email and password only.** Sign in calls `signInWithPassword`, create account calls `signUp`. There are no magic links and no OAuth, so no redirect URLs need to be configured.
- **Password length.** The project setting Authentication > Providers > Email > minimum password length is the server-side floor (Supabase default 6). The app enforces at least 8 characters before it calls Supabase.
- **"Confirm email" setting.** Off on the live project (`enable_confirmations = false` in `supabase/config.toml`).
  - Off: `signUp` returns a session and the user is signed in at once. A second sign-up with the same address answers `user_already_exists`; the app says "there is already an account for this address. sign in instead." and switches to sign in.
  - On: `signUp` returns a user but no session. The app shows "check your inbox to confirm your address, then sign in here." with a way back to sign in. An existing address then comes back as a user with no identities; the app shows the same neutral line so nobody learns which addresses exist.
- **Sessions stay on the device** in localStorage under the key `alltag.auth` (works in the Capacitor webview). supabase-js refreshes the token on its own.
- **Sign out keeps local data.** Only the session is removed; words, scenes and conversations stay on the phone.
- **Sync goes through `withSession`** in `src/sync/supabase.ts`. Signed out, it returns null and makes no network call.

## Keys

Only public values go to the client, as `VITE_*` vars: the Supabase project URL and anon key. No service role key is used or stored anywhere in the repo.

## One-time setup (human)

The hosted project is `alltag` in region eu-central-2 (Zurich).

1. **Supabase dashboard**
   - Authentication > Providers > Email: enabled, "Confirm email" off, minimum password length at least 6 (the app asks for 8).
   - Or from the CLI: `supabase config push` (reads `supabase/config.toml`).
2. **Schema**
   - `supabase link --project-ref <ref>`
   - `pnpm db:push` (runs `supabase db push`). This creates the tables, policies and the `scenes` bucket.
   - Optional: `pnpm db:types` writes generated types to `src/sync/database.types.ts`.
3. **Env vars**, in `.env` locally and in the Vercel project settings:
   - `VITE_SUPABASE_URL`: Project Settings > API > Project URL.
   - `VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`: Project Settings > API > anon public key.

Without these vars the app runs local-only and Settings says "sync is off in this build".

I built own auth on Supabase Auth and the full gate is green, but **I couldn't commit**: git is blocked by a leftover lock file, so all the changes are still uncommitted in the worktree.

**Blocker:** `/Users/k3ntaw/code/alltag/.git/worktrees/T-0064/index.lock` is empty, dated 16:02 (before my first git command), and no process has it open. It looks like a lock left behind by a git process that died. Your rules say deleting anything needs your approval, so I left it. If you say go, I'll `rm` that one file and then `git add -A && git commit` with the message "T-0064 U2 v4: own auth with Supabase Auth (password), our own sign-in screen, withSession for sync". To roll back after that, revert the commit and run `pnpm remove @supabase/supabase-js`. Nothing on the live project needs changing.

**Summary**
- `src/sync/supabase.ts`: one shared client, built only when the two Supabase env vars are set (read at call time). `withSession` returns null with no network call when signed out or unconfigured, if reading the session fails, or if refreshing an expiring session fails. Errors from `fn` pass through unchanged.
- `src/auth/auth.tsx`: sign-in status comes only from Supabase's auth events. If no event arrives within 4 s, it reads the stored session once with its own 3 s timeout, and offline that ends as signed out. Errors are mapped to calm copy by code first, then the offline check, then a generic line. The provider owns the Account overlay through `openAccount()` and `closeAccount()`.
- `src/screens/Account.tsx` is our own sign-in screen in the existing glass design. Settings has the new account section above the offline tutor. `main.tsx` wraps the app in the provider; `App.tsx` is unchanged.
- Docs and config: SUPABASE.md, `.env.example`, README and `supabase/config.toml` have the Clerk parts removed and the email sign-in settings added. Comments fixed in `schema.ts` and `seed.sql`. The applied migration and `migrations.test.ts` are untouched.

**Fixes from the review notes:**
1. The mock spreads the real `@supabase/supabase-js`, so `isAuthRetryableFetchError` stays real.
2. `AuthContext` is exported so Settings and Account tests can supply test values.
3. A missing or non-numeric `expires_at` triggers a refresh.
4. The 4 s fallback has its own 3 s timeout and ends as signed out.
5. The README names the three `VITE_` vars: `VITE_API_BASE`, `VITE_SUPABASE_URL`, `VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`.

**Two things I added beyond the spec:**
- `AuthResult` has an extra `existing` flag. Account uses it to switch to sign in when an address already has an account.
- A bad address shows "enter your email address". The spec gave no copy for that case.

**One new dependency:** `@supabase/supabase-js` 2.117.3, the one the spec names. `pnpm-lock.yaml` is the only lockfile.

- Modified: `.env.example`, `README.md`, `docs/SUPABASE.md`, `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `src/main.tsx`, `src/screens/Settings.tsx`, `src/screens/Settings.test.tsx`, `src/sync/schema.ts`, `supabase/config.toml`, `supabase/seed.sql`
- New: `src/auth/auth.tsx`, `src/auth/auth.test.tsx`, `src/screens/Account.tsx`, `src/screens/Account.test.tsx`, `src/sync/supabase.ts`, `src/sync/supabase.test.ts`
